🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.49% (7-year +21bp). At trading day 12 (last close) it was -1.49% against a five-campaign average of -0.23% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.35%. The 10-year is +25bp since the hike vs a +1bp campaign average at the same point.
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 678bp against a five-year average of 408bp (widest since May 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +56bp and BB +47bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.30 → 0.47 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • Stocks: Stocks closed Friday at records; Sunday futures point a little higher again.
  • FX: The dollar is steady; the euro keeps sliding below its longer-term trend.
  • Technicals: US stocks and Treasury yields are stretched unusually far above their averages.
  • Sectors: Tech alone is leading; banks, utilities and property have fallen hard this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Safer corporate debt still looks calm, but the riskiest junk bonds are under stress.
  • Crisis: Crisis risk is moderate, driven by Iran, oil, government debt and weak junk bonds.
  • Inflation: Underlying inflation is easing slowly, but price pressure is still too broad.
  • Tech Bubble: Stock prices are far below 2000 extremes, but easy money looks bubble-like.
  • Earnings & IPOs: PepsiCo and Delta lead earnings; I could not verify this week's IPOs.
  • Iran: The war continues with US strikes; I found no verified sign of a deal.
  • Warsh: Fed Chair Warsh leans hawkish; expect rates held high or raised further.
  • Week Ahead: Watch Monday's services survey, Wednesday's Fed minutes, and PepsiCo and Delta results.
  • Outlook: Mildly positive near term; more cautious over months as rates and junk stress bite.
  • Trades: Buy 10-year Treasuries, cut lowest-quality junk, hedge stocks cheaply, short the euro.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 buy, 22 hold long, 21 stay out

  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.

Sunday-evening futures are extending Friday's broad record-setting rally. ES is 7788.0 (+10.75), NQ is 31178.0 (+116.25) and Dow futures are 51508.0 (+31.0). Friday's cash closes were S&P 500 7722.72 (+56.27), Nasdaq 27190.86 (+319.26), Russell 2000 2832.895 (+26.27) and VIX 15.31 (-1.08). Treasuries are firm in early trade: TY is 104.453125 (+0.09375), after the US 10Y closed Friday at 5.2602% (-1.04bp). Oil is slightly softer, with WTI at 90.61 and Brent at 102.08. Gold (4157.16), silver (61.442) and copper (661.25) are all bid. Sentiment is clearly risk-on, but the rally is narrow and it is not the most important story. That story is the bottom of the junk-bond market. The computed HY contagion panel (as of 2026-10-01) has the Caa-minus-B spread gap at 678bp. That sits at the 99.6th percentile of its 5-year range, against a 5-year average of about 408bp, and is the widest since 2020-05-11. The FRED ICE CCC index is 1215bp, at its 100th percentile since 2023. Is it spreading up the quality ladder? Partly. Single-B OAS widened 56bp in a month to 310bp, and Ba widened 47bp to 195bp. But both are still near their 5-year averages (about 348bp and 219bp), so the move is a sharp widening from tight levels, not distress yet. The B-Ba gap of 115bp is below its 5-year average, which means BB and B are widening together rather than separating. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen to 0.47 from 0.30 three months ago, but it is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. Investment grade has barely moved (83bp, +3bp over 1m). This is descriptive, not a validated signal. The read is that CCC stress is real and lower-quality high yield is repricing, while the headline HY index (LF98OAS 3.06, tighter Friday) and IG are not yet affected. Two other things matter. A 10Y above 5.26% and a 30Y at 5.61% are pressuring rate-sensitive sectors: Financials -7.02% and Utilities -6.19% over 1m. And the Iran war and Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish stance keep tail risks in view ahead of Wednesday's FOMC minutes.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Rotation is very narrow and growth-led. US Info Tech is the only sector strongly positive across every window: 1d +1.06, 1w +1.44, 1m +7.06, YTD +30.13. Global Info Tech is similar at 1m +6.31 and YTD +37.49. Everything rate-sensitive or defensive has been hit over the past month. US Financials are -7.02 (global -7.68), Utilities -6.19, Real Estate -6.1, Materials -6.56, Cons Staples -4.06 and Health Care -3.75. That pattern fits a 5.26% 10Y punishing bond proxies, plus credit worries weighing on lenders. Financials are also -2.51 over 1w, so the CCC-spread widening is showing up in bank and lender equities. Energy keeps its YTD lead (US +37.49, global +32.23) on Iran-driven crude but has slipped over 1m (-2.55). Friday's breadth was better: Cons Discr +1.38, Materials +1.0 and Industrials +0.78. But one strong day does not change a month of defensive and cyclical-value weakness. In short, growth is beating value, and secular tech is beating both cyclicals and defensives. That is a concentration regime, not a broad-based bull market.

Headline credit is still priced for calm. US IG OAS is 0.82% (82bp), z -0.77, 7th percentile of history, above the historical minimum of 0.71%. US HY OAS is 3.06% (z -0.74, 17th percentile, -12bp Friday). EM USD OAS is 1.79% (z -1.21, 7th percentile), the tightest relative to its history. Europe is softer: EUR IG is 1.01% (+6bp Friday, 30th percentile) and EUR HY 3.48% (+9bp, 31st percentile). Measured against crisis peaks, US IG and EM score 0% of the GFC, EuroDebt, COVID and 2022 Hike peaks. US HY is only at 6% of the 2022 Hike widening, and EUR IG and EUR HY are at 15% and 13% of COVID. Underneath, the HY contagion panel (2026-10-01) shows clear stress at the bottom of the ratings scale. The Caa-B gap is 678bp, at the 99.6th percentile of 5 years and the widest since May 2020. Caa OAS is 988bp (+117bp 1m, +210bp 3m), and FRED CCC is 1215bp, at its 100th percentile since 2023. B OAS rose 56bp in 1m to 310bp and Ba rose 47bp to 195bp. The HY-IG gap is up 51bp in 1m to 235bp, but IG itself is only +3bp. The Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.47 from 0.30 three months ago but is still below its 0.70 5-year median. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. So far the contagion is partial: CCC distress is lifting B and BB from tight levels but has not reached IG. Key levels (analyst framing): US HY OAS through 3.50% and IG through 1.00% would confirm the stress is spreading upward. That would likely take a sustained equity drawdown, a 10Y above about 5.5%, or an oil shock from Iran. A return of the Caa-B gap toward its about 408bp 5-year average would signal the problem is staying contained. IG retesting its 0.71% historical low needs the current calm to persist and the CCC wave to stay idiosyncratic.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. This rule failed all three pre-registered gates as a tradable overlay (placebo p=0.465); do not size positions off it. See the monitor_spread skill (MONITOR_SPREAD.md).

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.82 vol points (44th percentile of the 34 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 107.3 (78th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 117bp (steeper by 45bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE

Right rim5.28%2026-09-30

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (90bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.28 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 56/100 — Underlying inflation is moderately persistent but easing at the margin. Every core-trend measure (median CPI, trimmed-mean CPI/PCE, median PCE, sticky CPI) is flagged 'falling', and z-scores sit near zero, so trend inflation is not accelerating. But it is also not at target. Median and trimmed-mean measures cluster around 2.2–2.7%, and sticky CPI is 2.74% while flexible CPI is 4.94%. Breadth is the problem: in the Dallas distribution, 28.9% of the PCE basket (computed: 13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5–10%) is rising faster than 5%, and only 25.8% is falling. Core PCE YoY of 3.00759% runs well above Core CPI's 2.4%, and the 1y breakeven of 2.7622% is above the 5y breakeven of 2.3828%. Markets expect near-term pressure, largely oil and tariff-related, to fade. For a hawkish Warsh Fed, this mix argues for no cuts, with inflation trending in the right direction but still too broad and still above target.

8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 60/100
Today is NOT at the March-2000 peak on equity froth, but it is AT or BEYOND 2000 conditions on the macro and complacency backdrop. In the Equity Froth dimension, the computed indicators show Nasdaq trailing P/E 39.07x at only 15% of the 2000 peak's 175x, the Nasdaq stretch vs its 200DMA at 20%, and semis (SOX P/E 45.06x) the frothiest component at 63%. Late-cycle catalysts are mixed. The 2s10s curve is 61% of the way to 2000's inversion, but IG and Baa spreads are tighter than in 2000 (131% and 166%), while ISM rollover readings are low (9% and 6%), so the cycle is not yet rolling over. In the Macro Regime dimension, commodities vs equities is at 200%, i.e. capital is crowded into equities beyond 2000, while the dollar is at 40%. Bear-market signposts show VIX complacency (200%) and loose financial conditions (NFCI 162%) beyond 2000 levels. AAII sentiment (20%), consumer confidence (17%) and margin growth (46%) are well short. Bottom line: the price-and-sentiment mania is mid-cycle, while the liquidity-and-complacency conditions are already at peak-cycle levels. The computed chart puts the current run at month 48 since Oct-2022 at 247.5. That is close to the dot-com path's 247.8 at month 53 in the 1990-anchored panel, which did not peak until month 113.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The analyst estimates here (top-10 S&P weight about 40%, CAPE about 39x, market cap/GDP about 215%, IPO froth about 40, LT EPS-growth signpost about 65) were NOT verified by web search this run, because the five-search budget went to Iran, Warsh, earnings, IPOs and the calendar. Treat them as rough judgment only. They suggest concentration and aggregate valuation (CAPE, market cap/GDP) are at or above 2000 levels even though the Nasdaq's own P/E is far lower. That gap exists because today's leaders have real earnings, while the 2000 Nasdaq P/E of 175x was inflated by profitless firms. The more relevant 2000 parallel is the setup, not the multiple: tight credit, loose financial conditions, low VIX, a narrow tech-led market (Info Tech +30.13% YTD while Financials, Utilities and Cons Discr are negative), and a central bank leaning hawkish into it. The CCC widening is the kind of late-cycle crack that showed up in 1998–2000 high yield well before equities peaked. It warrants caution, but historically it has been an early warning, not a timing signal.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

INFERENCE: hold at the next meeting with a hawkish bias, and a live option to hike again if core PCE (3.00759%) does not cool. At Jackson Hole (Aug 28) Warsh said recent softer prints had not meaningfully improved the underlying trend, and September hike odds rose above 50% afterward (Crypto Briefing). Wednesday's minutes from the Sep 15–16 FOMC meeting will show how many members back further tightening.

~1 YEAR

INFERENCE: higher for longer. No cuts are likely until trend inflation is clearly near 2%. Warsh has also long argued for a smaller Fed balance sheet and less forward guidance, so expect continued balance-sheet runoff and meeting-by-meeting, data-driven decisions. At Sintra (Jul 2) he said the Fed 'will not hand the market the answers in advance.' This favours a steeper curve and higher term premium, consistent with the 30Y at 5.6103%.

Warsh took the chair on May 22, 2026 and has used his major appearances (Sintra in July, Jackson Hole in August, and his semiannual testimony) to signal that the inflation fight is not over and that the Fed will not pre-commit. With the 2Y at 4.8122% and the 10Y at 5.2602%, markets have priced a hawkish Fed. The risk for the coming meetings is whether CCC credit stress and a 7% monthly drop in Financials make him less aggressive. His record as a 2008-era governor suggests he will separate financial-stability tools from rate policy. That is my inference and is not stated in the sources.
